name: Sea moss / chlorella / spirulina

lead: Sea moss (Irish moss), chlorella and spirulina are algae products sold as superfood supplements for general wellness, skin and energy.
Public health sources say evidence is insufficient to recommend them for any human condition, and no studies were found testing them for appearance.

paras: They are nutrient-dense foods (protein, minerals, carrageenan in sea moss), and proponents attribute wider benefits to this content; published research has not established such effects.

Reported concerns include microcystin and heavy-metal contamination of some products, allergic reactions, drug interactions, high iodine in sea moss, and FDA warning letters over false health claims for chlorella products.

lead: Sea moss, chlorella and spirulina are algae-based products sold as dietary supplements and 'superfoods'. Sea moss usually refers to Irish moss (Chondrus crispus), a red seaweed of North Atlantic coasts rich in the thickener carrageenan [1]. Chlorella is a genus of single-celled green algae [2], and spirulina is the dried biomass of cyanobacteria, mainly of the genus Arthrospira [3].

They are promoted in wellness and appearance-oriented circles for general nutrition, skin, energy and 'detox'. Public health bodies have not endorsed these uses: the US National Institutes of Health has said the evidence is insufficient to recommend spirulina for any human condition [3], and the American Cancer Society has said available studies do not support chlorella for preventing or treating disease [2].

paras: Irish moss is a red alga whose dry weight is roughly 55 percent carrageenan, with protein, minerals and notable iodine and sulfur content. When boiled it forms a gel that can hold many times its weight in water, and it has long been used in puddings in Scotland and Ireland, while carrageenan is an industrial food thickener [1].

Spirulina has been harvested historically, for example by the Aztecs from Lake Texcoco and by the Kanembu people near Lake Chad, with large-scale production studied from the 1970s [3]. Dried spirulina is high in protein, but its vitamin B12 is mostly an inactive form, and the American Dietetic Association (2009) said it is not a reliable B12 source [3]. Chlorella was promoted in the mid-twentieth century as a solution to world hunger, but its indigestible cell wall and low energy capture limited that idea, and it has since been sold mainly as a health food [2].

Some cyanobacteria produce toxins called microcystins. Spirulina does not make them, but contaminated batches can contain them, and Health Canada set a limit for microcystin-LR in finished products. Heavy-metal contamination of some spirulina products, including lead, has also been reported [3]. Spirulina may interact with immune-related or blood-clotting medications and contains phenylalanine, and a 2024 review identified a small number of allergy cases including anaphylaxis [3].

Chlorella cell walls have been reported to contain lipopolysaccharides that may affect the immune system, although later work suggests these differ from those of Gram-negative bacteria [2]. The US FDA has issued warning letters to supplement companies for falsely advertising health benefits of chlorella products [2]. Sea moss is rich in iodine, and available sources do not give intake guidance [1].

No studies found examining sea moss, chlorella or spirulina for skin, facial appearance or other looksmaxxing outcomes. Related general-health research is limited: the European Food Safety Authority rejected claimed blood-glucose benefits of spirulina in 2013, and HIV studies found no conclusive effect on mortality, weight or immune response [3].
